cells.tense: You set the shape down and it holds where the mix keeps moving.
cells.act: notice what you already know before you reason about it
cells.ask: Before you arrange the next thing, write the first read of it in a line — then let that line sit beside the arranging and see if it still rings true.
cells.core:
You can give shape to four things at once and keep adjusting the mix without losing any of them. When the plans are scattered, you lay down the frame that work happens inside, and nothing about it feels heavy, because the frame keeps moving with what shifts. Most people manage the structure or the tuning. You're doing both, and the result is quiet: something holds that didn't before.

The one thing that slips in a role like this is which part actually matters right now. You can build a perfectly fair arrangement around the wrong priority and not notice until it's load-bearing. So before you organize the next thing, write the first read of it in a line, before the reasons start talking. That first read usually names the piece everything else should hang on. Begin there, and the arranging you spend lands on the part that counts.
cells.sheetLine: You'd rather adjust a shape than leave it unsettled.
cells.verb: Turning loose pieces into a shape that holds
cells.place: Where you're always adjusting the mix, reading whether to add or ease off

cells.tense: You'll have the whole shape built before the pieces have shown what they are.
cells.act: step back far enough to see the whole arrangement
cells.ask: Next time an arrangement feels so clear you want to fix it in place, step back and describe the whole shape to yourself before deciding anything — say what it is doing, not what you want it to do.
cells.core:
Something in one part of your life is being organized into a shape it hasn't grown into yet — a schedule, a role, a way of running the thing — and from where you're standing it looks like care. You can feel the whole structure behind it, and you want the outside to match the inside now. So you set the version that's two seasons past anyone's timing. Then you shore up what should have been loosened, and you're managing the arrangement instead of living in what it holds.

Less structure isn't the answer. Seeing the shape instead of living inside it is. Next time it feels obvious, step back and describe the whole arrangement — the shape, not this case — and decide nothing. The mechanism gets clearer and quieter, so it can keep adjusting. Whatever you build after that keeps its hinges and fits what's actually there.

cells.tense: The pieces were put down and never picked back up.
cells.act: clear the ground of what came down
cells.ask: Go to a surface where things came apart and stayed that way — a desk, a shelf, a folder — and clear it without starting anything new there.
cells.core:
A structure that used to carry something stopped, and the pieces are still where they fell. You've built around the pile instead of on it — new habits, small workarounds, pieces shifted here and there — and you couldn't say when the original arrangement ended. Which is why the parts won't assemble. There's no clear ground to lay them on.

This turns fast when it turns. Go to one surface — a desk, a shelf, a folder — and clear what came undone. Put away what you're keeping, bin what you're done with, and start nothing to fill the space. The first step is the one you'd skip, and it's the whole job. In ten minutes you'll have a surface. New structures go up much faster on cleared ground than on crowded wreckage.

cells.tense: People are moving in an order you're keeping for them without knowing you set it.
cells.act: mark the end of it with a plain act
cells.ask: Pick an arrangement you've kept going for other people that you're done carrying, and mark its end plainly — a last note, a date set, nothing ceremonial.
cells.core:
People are standing in a shape you made. They move when you move. At work, in the family, wherever the schedule runs through you, things work because you're quietly holding the frame — and you'd tell anyone you're barely keeping up. Ask you what you do and this wouldn't come up. It isn't seen as work you do, because it works too well to be noticed, including by you.

Some of what you're carrying is already over. Pick an arrangement you've kept going for other people that you're done carrying, and mark its end plainly — a last note, a date set, nothing ceremonial. The weight is there either way. What changes is that the closing is yours, so you're holding something you chose rather than something you can't put down.

cells.verb: Turning loose pieces into a shape that holds
cells.place: Where you're always adjusting the mix, reading whether to add or ease off

The reader is most likely to object to the Too Little cell — 'I'm not disorganized, I just have too much to do' — so that ask plants one wanted thing rather than diagnosing the whole person. The ask survives being wrong because it produces a small real clearing either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any version of 'things make sense in your presence' as a promise about the reader's future rather than a description of the balanced face; it is kept out of the cells and only named here.
